---
title: "College, Measured in Hours of Work"
subtitle: "Tuition grew three times faster than pay for 35 years. Then, quietly, it stopped."
author: "SixtyEight95"
date: "2026-11-13"

---

```{r setup}
source("../../R/fred.R")
source("../../R/education_data.R")
library(plotly)
library(knitr)

times <- function(x) paste0(formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1), "×")
since_1980 <- growth_since(1980)
since_peak <- growth_since(hours_peak$year)
twist_drop <- 1 - college_now$hours_index / hours_peak$hours_index
months_label <- paste(format(latest_month %m-% months(11), "%B %Y"), "to", format(latest_month, "%B %Y"))
```

If there's one cost that defines "things were easier for our parents," it's college. We wanted to know how
much harder it really got, and whether it's still getting worse. So we measured it the SixtyEight95 way:
**in hours of work.**

## The short answer

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Since 1980, college tuition has grown **`r times(since_1980$tuition)`**. Hourly pay grew `r times(since_1980$wages)`, and
prices for everything else grew `r times(since_1980$prices)`. So a year of college takes **about
`r round(college_now$hours_index / 100, 1)` times as many hours of work** as it did in 1980.

But here's what almost nobody talks about: **college peaked in `r hours_peak$year`.** Since then, pay has grown
faster than tuition, and a year of college now takes about **`r round(twist_drop * 100)`% fewer hours of work** than
at the peak.
:::

## How we measure "hours of work" here

For groceries and housing, we could use actual prices. For college, the government doesn't publish one
national "price of college," because it varies so much: a community college and a private university are
worlds apart. What it does publish is a **price index**, which tracks how much tuition and fees have changed over time
for the same kinds of schools.

So we set **1980 = 100 hours** and asked: if a year of college took 100 hours of work in 1980, how many
hours would the same year of college take in every year since? It's a measure of *change*, not a price
tag, and it works for any school.

## 45 years of college, in hours of work

```{r hours chart}
#| fig-height: 4.5
p <- ggplot(college_yearly, aes(year, hours_index, group = 1,
            text = paste0(year, ": ", round(hours_index), " hours",
                          "<br>(1980 = 100 hours)"))) +
  geom_line(color = "#1F4E5A", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Hours of work (1980 = 100)")

ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text") %>% config(displayModeBar = FALSE)
```

From 1980 to `r hours_peak$year`, the line almost only goes up. At the peak, a year of college took
**`r round(hours_peak$hours_index)` hours** for every 100 it took in 1980. Today it's **`r round(college_now$hours_index)`**.

## Tuition vs. pay vs. everything else

```{r growth chart}
#| fig-height: 4.5
growth <- college_monthly %>%
  mutate(`College tuition` = tuition / mean(tuition[year(date) == 1980]),
         `Hourly pay`      = wage    / mean(wage[year(date) == 1980]),
         `Everything else` = cpi     / mean(cpi[year(date) == 1980])) %>%
  select(date, `College tuition`, `Hourly pay`, `Everything else`) %>%
  pivot_longer(-date, names_to = "series", values_to = "times")

p2 <- ggplot(growth, aes(date, times, color = series, group = series,
             text = paste0(series, ", ", format(date, "%b %Y"), ": ", times(times), " the 1980 level"))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("College tuition" = "#C05621", "Hourly pay" = "#1F4E5A",
                                "Everything else" = "grey55")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Times the 1980 level", color = NULL)

ggplotly(p2, tooltip = "text") %>%
  layout(legend = list(orientation = "h", y = 1.1)) %>%
  config(displayModeBar = FALSE)
```

Hourly pay and general prices moved almost together for 45 years. College tuition went off on its own.

Researchers point to several reasons for the long climb, including states cutting per-student funding for
public colleges (especially after the 2008 recession, which shifted more of the cost onto students), rising
demand for degrees, and colleges spending more on staff and facilities.

## The twist: college has been getting easier to afford

Since `r hours_peak$year`, tuition is up `r round((since_peak$tuition - 1) * 100)`% while pay is up `r round((since_peak$wages - 1) * 100)`%.
That gap is why the hours-of-work line has been falling for almost a decade.

Two things drove it:

- **Tuition growth slowed down.** Many public universities froze or capped tuition, and enrollment has been
  soft, which limits how much schools can raise prices.
- **Pay sped up.** Wages for regular workers grew quickly from 2021 to 2023, faster than they had in years.

College is still far more expensive in work time than it was in 1980. But the story of "it only ever gets
worse" isn't true anymore.

## Snapshot by year

```{r table}
college_yearly %>%
  filter(year %in% c(1980, 1990, 2000, 2008, hours_peak$year, 2019, 2022, year(latest_month))) %>%
  transmute(Year = ifelse(year == year(latest_month), paste(year, "(so far)"), as.character(year)),
            `Tuition vs 1980` = times(tuition / college_yearly$tuition[college_yearly$year == 1980]),
            `Pay vs 1980`     = times(wage / college_yearly$wage[college_yearly$year == 1980]),
            `Prices vs 1980`  = times(cpi / college_yearly$cpi[college_yearly$year == 1980]),
            `Hours of work (1980 = 100)` = round(hours_index)) %>%
  kable(align = "lrrrr")
```

## The fine print

- **This is a price index, not a bill.** It tracks how tuition and fees changed, not what any one school
  charges.
- **Grants and scholarships vary.** Many families pay less than the posted price, and how much less has
  changed over time.
- **Tuition isn't the whole cost.** Housing, food, and books are separate, and housing near campus has its own
  story.
- **Pay is the average worker's, before taxes.** It's the same pay measure we use in every SixtyEight95
  "hours of work" story, so they're comparable.

## The bottom line

College went from expensive to very expensive between 1980 and `r hours_peak$year`, rising far faster than
paychecks. Since then, the trend has quietly reversed. A year of college still takes nearly three times the
work it did in 1980, but less than it did a decade ago.

---

**How we did this.** College costs are the Consumer Price Index for "college tuition and fees" (BLS series
CUUR0000SEEB01) from the [Bureau of Labor Statistics](https://www.bls.gov/cpi/). "Everything else" is the CPI
for all items, and pay is average hourly earnings of production and nonsupervisory employees (about 80% of
private-sector workers), both via [FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/). Hours of work = tuition index ÷
hourly pay, scaled so 1980 = 100. "Today" is the average of `r months_label`. BLS did not collect
October 2025 prices during the federal government shutdown, so that month is skipped.
